title: Reading eight side chains
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) All eight amino acids are drawn as they exist at physiological pH (about 7.4).

(나) Panels A–G share the same backbone; only the side chain below the α carbon differs.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Side chains C and D carry opposite full charges, so they can form an ionic bond if folding brings them together.
statements.explanation: C's –COO- is negative (acidic) and D's –NH3+ is positive (basic); opposite charges attract.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: B can hydrogen-bond with water through its –OH, even though it carries no full charge.
statements.explanation: Oxygen is electronegative, so the –OH is polar: B is a polar, uncharged, hydrophilic side chain.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: In a folded water-soluble protein, G's side chain would most likely be found buried in the interior.
statements.explanation: A CH2 plus a benzene ring is all carbon and hydrogen — nonpolar and hydrophobic — so it clusters away from water inside the fold.

links: R-group classes · Ionic bonds between side chains · Polarity from electronegativity (Module 2)

title: Which side chain fits?
prompt: Using the diagram, match each description to the side chain that fits it.

pairs.left: Gives the backbone the most freedom to rotate and bend
Restricts rotation of the backbone, limiting folding around it
pairs.right: H: ring bonded back to the nitrogen

pairs.left: Can form a covalent cross-bridge with another copy of itself
Positively charged at physiological pH
Polar but uncharged; hydrogen-bonds with water

explanation: F is glycine (side chain H): tiny, so the C–N bond rotates freely. H is proline: its side chain loops back to the amino nitrogen and locks rotation. E is cysteine: two –SH groups can join as an S–S disulfide bridge. D is lysine (basic, +). B is serine: its –OH is polar but uncharged.
links: Special amino acids: glycine, proline, cysteine · Charged vs polar side chains

box: In the diagram, H's side chain is bonded to the backbone at two points: the α carbon and the nitrogen.
claim: Because its side chain forms a ring, H gives the backbone more freedom to rotate than F does.
explanation: The ring locks the N–Cα bond, restricting rotation and limiting folding around proline (H). F (glycine, side chain –H) is the most flexible: its tiny side chain lets the C–N bond rotate freely.
links: Proline restricts rotation · Glycine adds flexibility

stem: A protein engineer replaces a glycine in a tight hairpin turn with alanine (side chain –CH3). The protein no longer folds correctly. Which explanation fits best?
options: Alanine's side chain is charged and repels nearby side chains in the turn
Alanine's side chain bonds back to its own backbone nitrogen, closing a ring
Its side chain limits backbone rotation, so the chain can't bend as sharply
Alanine forms a disulfide bridge that locks the turn in the wrong place
Alanine can't form peptide bonds because its α carbon is asymmetric
explanation: Glycine's side chain is just H, so the backbone can rotate freely about the C–N bond — the flexibility a tight turn needs. Even a small –CH3 restricts that rotation. Alanine is nonpolar and uncharged, has no –SH for disulfides and no ring (that's proline), and every amino acid forms peptide bonds.
links: Glycine flexibility · Sequence determines folding

box: Collagen, the main protein of bone and tendon, is a tight triple helix. Every third amino acid is glycine, and each glycine sits at the crowded centre where the three chains meet.
claim: A mutation replacing one of these glycines with a bulkier amino acid can weaken collagen, because only glycine's single H atom fits in that central position.
explanation: Glycine has the smallest side chain (H). A larger side chain can't pack into the helix centre and distorts the triple helix — the cause of many cases of osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease).
links: Glycine: the smallest side chain · Real-world: brittle bone disease

box: A perm breaks the disulfide bonds in hair keratin with a reducing agent, holds the hair around curlers, then re-forms disulfide bonds with an oxidizing agent.
claim: The curl lasts because the disulfide bonds re-form between exactly the same pairs of cysteines as before.
explanation: While the hair is held in its new shape, cysteines that weren't partners before sit side by side, and the oxidizer links them into new S–S bridges. Covalent bridges in new positions hold the new shape; re-forming the old pairs would simply restore the original shape.
links: Disulfide cross-bridges · Real-world: perms

stem: The peptide Val–Gly–Ala–His–Lys is assembled from free amino acids by condensation reactions. How many water molecules are released, and which amino acid carries the free amino group?
options: 5 water molecules; Val
4 water molecules; Lys
5 water molecules; Lys
3 water molecules; Val
4 water molecules; Val
explanation: Five amino acids are joined by 4 peptide bonds, and each dehydration releases one H2O. Sequences are written from the amino (N) end to the carboxyl (C) end, so Val, written first, keeps the free amino group, and Lys keeps the free carboxyl group.
links: Peptide bonds form by dehydration · N- and C-terminus · Writing sequences N→C

box: One lab reports a tripeptide as K-G-V. Another lab reports a tripeptide as V-G-K.
claim: These are the same molecule: both contain lysine, glycine and valine, just written from opposite ends.
explanation: Sequences are written from the N-terminus to the C-terminus. K-G-V has lysine at the free amino end; V-G-K has valine there and lysine at the carboxyl end. A backbone has direction (amino end ≠ carboxyl end), so these are different peptides.
links: Primary structure is written N→C · Polypeptides have direction

stem: Using the diagram, a side chain on a protein's surface changes from D to B. What is the main change at that spot?
options: It becomes negatively charged and repels nearby negative groups
It loses its positive charge but can still hydrogen-bond with water
It becomes nonpolar and tends to move into the folded protein's interior
It gains the ability to form a disulfide bridge with another copy
Nothing changes, since both side chains end in a polar group
explanation: D (–(CH2)4–NH3+, lysine) is basic and positively charged at physiological pH; B (–CH2–OH, serine) is polar but uncharged. The spot loses its positive charge — and any ionic bond it made — but B's –OH still hydrogen-bonds with water, so it can stay at the surface.
links: Basic vs polar side chains · Charge at physiological pH

box: A protein drug clumps together in its storage vial. Its designers find two valines (side chain –CH(CH3)2) exposed on its surface and replace them with lysines (side chain –(CH2)4–NH3+).
claim: The swap should make the clumping worse, because the new charged side chains will stick to nonpolar patches on neighbouring drug molecules.
explanation: The reverse: exposed nonpolar side chains are what make the molecules stick, since water pushes nonpolar groups together. Charged lysines interact with water (and repel each other), so the swap makes the surface more hydrophilic and the drug clumps less.
links: Hydrophobic vs charged side chains · Real-world: protein drug formulation

box: Proteins are built from 20 kinds of amino acids, like words built from an alphabet.
claim: A chain only 3 amino acids long already has 8,000 possible sequences.
explanation: Each of the 3 positions can hold any of 20 amino acids: 20 × 20 × 20 = 8,000. For a 300-amino-acid protein the number is 20^300 — one reason proteins can be so diverse and versatile.
links: 20 amino acids as an alphabet · Protein diversity

title: One backbone, twenty personalities
stem: Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Every amino acid has an amino group, a carboxyl group and an H bonded to its α carbon; only the fourth group, the R group, differs.

(나) At physiological pH, a free amino acid carries H3N+ and COO-.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Because of (나), every amino acid in a folded protein carries both an H3N+ and a COO- on its backbone.
statements.explanation: Inside a chain, the amino and carboxyl groups are used up in peptide bonds. Only the first amino acid keeps a free amino group (N-terminus) and only the last keeps a free carboxyl group (C-terminus).

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Two different proteins of the same length share the same repeating backbone (N–C–C–N–C–C…); they differ only in the side chains attached to it.
statements.explanation: Peptide bonds always join the same backbone atoms, so sequence differences show up only in the R groups sticking out from the chain.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Proline is the only amino acid whose α carbon carries two identical groups.
statements.explanation: That's glycine, whose R group is a second H — so its α carbon isn't asymmetric. Proline's α carbon carries four different groups; its side chain loops back to the nitrogen.

links: Amino acid structure · Charged ends at physiological pH · N- and C-terminus

stem: Using the diagram, which pair of side chains, brought together by folding, could join two parts of a protein with a covalent bond?
options: E and E (two –CH2–SH groups)
C and D (–COO- and –NH3+)
B and B (two –CH2–OH groups)
A and G (–CH3 and the ring)
F and F (two –H atoms)
explanation: Two cysteine –SH groups can be joined into an S–S disulfide bond — a covalent cross-bridge, far stronger than the ionic bond C and D can form, the hydrogen bonds between B's –OH groups, or the weak van der Waals contacts between nonpolar A and G.
links: Disulfide bonds are covalent · Bond strengths (Module 2)

box: Keratin in hair, the enzyme amylase in saliva, and antibodies in blood are all proteins with very different jobs.
claim: Their different jobs come mainly from different kinds of bonds in their backbones rather than from their amino acid sequences.
explanation: All proteins share the same backbone, linked by the same peptide bonds. What differs is the sequence of side chains, which folds each chain into its own shape — and shape determines function.
links: Proteins are diverse and versatile · Sequence → shape → function

title: Two backbone patterns
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The helix and the sheet are parts of the same protein.

(나) Each R marks a side chain sticking out from the backbone.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Every dashed bond links a backbone C=O to a backbone N–H; none involves an R group.
statements.explanation: Secondary structure comes from hydrogen bonds between backbone groups of nearby amino acids; side chains aren't part of these bonds.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The sheet's two strands are parallel, since they lie side by side.
statements.explanation: Side by side doesn't mean the same direction: the top strand runs N→C left to right and the bottom strand right to left, so they're antiparallel. Sheets can be either.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: In the helix, the C=O of residue 3 bonds to the N–H of residue 7.
statements.explanation: Each C=O bonds to the N–H four residues along (1–5, 2–6, 3–7…), which ties each turn of the helix to the next.

links: Secondary structure: backbone H-bonds only · α helix · β sheet

box: An isolated 11-residue segment folds into the helix in the diagram, with residue 1 at its N-terminus.
claim: Residues 8–11 have their N–H groups hydrogen-bonded within the segment, but their C=O groups have no partner.
explanation: Each C=O of residue n pairs with the N–H of residue n + 4. Residues 8–11 would need partners 12–15, which don't exist, while their own N–H groups receive bonds from residues 4–7. At the other end, residues 1–4 have unpaired N–H groups.
links: α helix: residue n bonds to n + 4

stem: Proline's side chain bonds to its own backbone nitrogen, so in a chain that nitrogen carries no H. If residue 9 of the helix in the diagram were proline, which hydrogen bond could not form?
options: The one between residue 6's C=O and residue 10's N–H
The one between residue 4's C=O and residue 8's N–H
The one between residue 7's C=O and residue 11's N–H
The one between residue 5's C=O and residue 9's N–H
None, since helix H-bonds involve only backbone atoms
explanation: Residue 9's N–H is the partner of residue 5's C=O (n to n + 4). Proline has no N–H to give, so that bond is lost. Here a side chain matters after all: proline's ring changes a backbone atom itself, one reason proline disrupts helices.
links: α helix pattern · Proline restricts the backbone

title: What holds the fold together?
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) One sample is treated with a reducing agent that turns each –S–S– back into two –SH groups.

(나) A second sample is moved from pH 7 into strong acid (pH 1).

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: In (나), contact B gets stronger, because the extra H+ adds positive charge to both of its groups.
statements.explanation: COO- picks up H+ and becomes uncharged COOH, so the attraction between opposite charges at B is lost, not strengthened.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: In (나), contact D is lost, because its nonpolar groups pick up H+ and become charged.
statements.explanation: Nonpolar groups such as –CH3 don't gain or lose H+ at all, so pH leaves D intact. pH acts on ionizable groups like those at B.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (가) breaks contact A but leaves the protein's primary structure unchanged.
statements.explanation: A disulfide bridge links two side chains; it isn't part of the backbone, so the amino acid sequence (held by peptide bonds) is untouched.

links: Tertiary interactions · Disulfide vs ionic bonds · pH and ionization (Module 2)

title: Four ways to unfold a protein
prompt: Using the diagram, match each treatment to the contact it most directly disrupts.

pairs.left: A reducing agent that adds H to each sulfur
Concentrated salt, whose ions crowd around charged groups
Urea, which hydrogen-bonds to polar groups in place of their partners
A detergent whose nonpolar tails coat nonpolar groups

explanation: Each treatment targets one interaction type: reducing agents split covalent disulfides (A); ions shield the charges of an ionic bond (B); urea competes for hydrogen bonds (C); detergents surround nonpolar groups so they no longer need to hide from water (D).
links: Tertiary interactions · Bond types (Module 2) · Denaturation

box: In the diagram, contact D sits in the middle of the fold, surrounded by the chain, while water lies outside.
claim: D holds together mainly because nonpolar groups attract one another strongly, much as the opposite charges at B do.
explanation: Nonpolar groups attract one another only weakly (van der Waals forces). They cluster mainly because water molecules hydrogen-bond with each other and push nonpolar groups aside (Module 2), so the groups end up hidden in the interior.
links: Hydrophobic interior · Water drives nonpolar clustering (Module 2)

stem: An enzyme is a homodimer: two identical chains held together by side-chain contacts. A mutation changes one amino acid on the surface where the two chains touch. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Nothing changes, since surface amino acids don't affect quaternary structure
The two chains now differ in sequence, so the enzyme becomes a heterodimer
Each chain can still fold, but the pair may not assemble into the enzyme
The peptide bonds that join the two chains to each other are broken
The chains form a disulfide bridge at that spot, locking them together
explanation: Subunits are held together by the same side-chain interactions as tertiary structure, so a changed contact residue can block pairing. Both chains come from the same mutated gene, so they're still identical (still a homodimer), and subunits aren't joined by peptide bonds.
links: Quaternary structure · Homodimer vs heterodimer

box: Insulin consists of two short chains, A and B, cut from one longer precursor polypeptide after it has folded.
claim: In mature insulin, the A and B chains are joined end to end by peptide bonds.
explanation: Once the connecting segment is cut out, the chains are held together by two disulfide bonds — covalent bridges between cysteine side chains, not backbone peptide bonds. Cutting an inactive precursor into its active form is also a post-translational modification.
links: Disulfide bridges between chains · Post-translational cleavage

stem: An enzyme is unfolded with chemicals that break its hydrogen bonds and disulfide bonds, leaving its peptide bonds intact. When the chemicals are slowly removed, the chain refolds into its active shape. What does this show?
options: The amino acid sequence alone holds the information for the folded shape
The enzyme's shape was stored in disulfide bonds that survived the treatment
Peptide bonds broke and re-formed in their original order
Refolding needed a correctly folded copy of the enzyme as a template
Secondary and tertiary structure don't depend on the sequence
explanation: Nothing but the sequence (primary structure) remained, yet the original shape returned, so primary structure determines secondary and tertiary structure. (A cooked egg white can't refold because its unfolded chains tangle into aggregates instead.)
links: Primary structure determines higher levels · Denaturation and refolding

box: A peptide alternates nonpolar valine with charged lysine or glutamate: Val–Lys–Val–Glu–Val–Lys–Val–Glu.
claim: Stretched out as a strand, all its valine side chains point to one side and all its charged side chains to the other.
explanation: R groups alternate sides along an extended chain, so residues 1, 3, 5 and 7 (Val) share one side and residues 2, 4, 6 and 8 the other — one nonpolar face and one charged face. Such a strand can lie with its nonpolar face against the protein interior and its charged face toward water.
links: R groups alternate sides · Nonpolar and charged faces

box: In the diagram's sheet, a third strand is added below the bottom strand, running from N at the left to C at the right.
claim: The new strand is antiparallel to the bottom strand and parallel to the top strand.
explanation: The bottom strand runs N→C right to left and the top strand left to right. A strand running left to right is opposite to the bottom strand (antiparallel) and matches the top one (parallel). Both arrangements occur in sheets.
links: β sheets: parallel and antiparallel strands

stem: In the diagram's sheet, R groups alternate between above the sheet (filled) and below it (hollow). The sheet lies against the protein's nonpolar interior on one face, with water on the other. Which pattern along each strand fits best?
options: Nonpolar side chains at every position along the strand
Charged side chains at every position along the strand
Nonpolar side chains on one strand, polar side chains on the other
Glycine at every position so that the sheet can bend
Nonpolar and polar side chains alternating along the strand
explanation: Consecutive residues point to opposite faces, so alternating nonpolar and polar residues put every nonpolar side chain on the interior face and every polar one on the water face. An all-nonpolar strand would leave half its side chains facing water.
links: R groups alternate sides · Faces of a β sheet

title: Which level of structure?
prompt: Match each observation to the level of protein structure it describes.

pairs.left: A mutation swaps the 6th amino acid of the chain for a different one
Part of a keratin chain coils into a right-handed spiral held by backbone hydrogen bonds
The helices and sheets of one enzyme chain pack together around a core of nonpolar side chains
Two identical chains must pair up before an enzyme works

explanation: Primary = the sequence; secondary = local backbone H-bond patterns (α helix, β sheet); tertiary = the whole folded shape of one chain, set by its side chains (here, nonpolar ones hiding in the core); quaternary = how separate chains (subunits) assemble.
links: Four levels of protein structure

title: From gene to anticodon
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The four rows show one codon's worth of a gene, its mRNA and the tRNA that reads it.

(나) Unlabelled sequences are written 5'→3'.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The mRNA is copied from the nontemplate strand, which is why their sequences match.
statements.explanation: RNA polymerase reads the template strand. The mRNA matches the nontemplate strand only because both are complementary to the template (Module 4).

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Written in the standard 5'→3' direction, the anticodon is UGC.
statements.explanation: The anticodon is 3'-CGU-5'; read from its 5' end it is 5'-UGC-3'.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The anticodon has the same sequence and orientation as the DNA template strand, except that it has U where the template has T.
statements.explanation: The template strand and the anticodon are both complementary to the codon, so they match base for base (3'-CGT-5' vs 3'-CGU-5'), with U in RNA where DNA has T.

links: Codon–anticodon pairing is antiparallel · Template vs nontemplate strand (Module 4)

box: In the diagram, the middle base of the DNA template strand (G) is mutated to A. (GCA = Ala, GUA = Val, GAA = Glu)
claim: The mRNA codon becomes GUA, so the protein carries valine in place of alanine.
explanation: The template's middle base pairs with the codon's middle base. Template G → A means the mRNA gets U instead of C: GCA becomes GUA, which codes for Val. One base change in the gene, one amino acid change in the protein.
links: Template strand → codon → amino acid

stem: Using the genetic code table, which single-base change in the mRNA codon CUU would NOT change the amino acid?
options: CUU → CCU
CUU → CUC
CUU → AUU
CUU → CAU
CUU → UUU
explanation: CUU and CUC both code for Leu. The others give Pro (CCU), Ile (AUU), His (CAU) and Phe (UUU). Third-position changes are the ones most often silent, because the code is redundant: many amino acids have codons that differ only in their third base.
links: Redundancy of the genetic code · Silent changes

box: Using the genetic code table, count the codons for each amino acid.
claim: Every amino acid is encoded by at least two codons, which is what makes the code redundant.
explanation: Methionine (AUG) and tryptophan (UGG) each have only one codon. The code is still redundant because most amino acids have two to six codons: 61 coding codons for 20 amino acids.
links: Redundancy of the genetic code · AUG start codon

stem: Using the genetic code table, a ribosome starts at the first AUG of the mRNA 5'-CCAUGGUUCAUUGAGC-3'. What polypeptide is made?
options: Met–Val–His–Trp (4 amino acids)
Pro–Trp–Phe–Ile–Glu (5 amino acids)
Met–Val (2 amino acids)
Met–Val–His (3 amino acids)
Met–Val–His–Stop (4 amino acids)
explanation: Starting at AUG sets the reading frame: AUG (Met) GUU (Val) CAU (His) UGA (stop). A stop codon has no amino acid (and UGA is not UGG, Trp), so the chain is 3 long. Reading from the first base would give a different frame (CCA UGG UUC…) and a different protein.
links: Start codon sets the reading frame · Stop codons

stem: Which mutation in the middle of a gene's coding sequence is least likely to destroy the protein's function?
options: Deleting a single nucleotide from the middle of a codon
Inserting two nucleotides between two codons
Inserting one nucleotide just after the start codon
Deleting the three nucleotides of one whole codon
Changing one codon in the middle to UAA
explanation: Codons are read three at a time from the start codon. Removing one whole codon deletes one amino acid but keeps the reading frame, so everything downstream is unchanged. Adding or removing 1 or 2 nucleotides shifts the frame and garbles every later codon, and UAA ends the chain early.
links: Reading frame · Nonoverlapping triplets · Stop codons

title: Freeze-frame on a ribosome
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) UGG codes for Trp and AAA for Lys; UAG is a stop codon.

(나) The ribosome will keep translating this mRNA until the polypeptide is finished.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The incoming tRNA marked ? must carry the anticodon 3'-ACC-5' and the amino acid Trp.
statements.explanation: The A site holds codon 5'-UGG-3'; its antiparallel partner is 3'-ACC-5', and the tRNA with that anticodon is charged with Trp.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The finished polypeptide will be Met–Ala–Trp–Lys, with Met at its N-terminus.
statements.explanation: AUG GCU UGG AAA, then UAG (stop): Met–Ala–Trp–Lys. Met, the first amino acid, keeps the free amino group.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The tRNA in the E site is uncharged and is about to leave the ribosome.
statements.explanation: It delivered Met, passed it on when the first peptide bond formed, and now exits empty from the E site.

links: A, P and E sites · Codon–anticodon pairing · Start and stop codons

stem: In the diagram, which way is the ribosome moving along the mRNA, and how can you tell?
options: Toward 5': tRNA anticodons are written 3'→5'
Toward 5': Met at the chain's free end was the last amino acid added
Toward 3': the large subunit always sits on the mRNA's 3' side
It stays put while the mRNA slides back and forth through it
Toward 3': the start codon AUG has already moved into the E site
explanation: Ribosomes read mRNA 5'→3'. The start codon AUG — read first — is already in the E site, and the unread codons lie on the 3' side. Met at the chain's free end was the first amino acid added, not the last, which also shows the ribosome began at the 5' end.
links: Ribosomes move 5'→3' · A, P and E sites · The N-terminus is made first

box: In a classic experiment, the cysteine already attached to a charged tRNA-Cys was chemically converted to alanine, leaving the tRNA's anticodon unchanged. The tRNA was then added to a protein-making system.
claim: Alanine was inserted wherever the mRNA had a cysteine codon, because the ribosome checks only codon–anticodon pairing, not which amino acid the tRNA carries.
explanation: tRNAs are adapters: the anticodon reads the codon, and the amino acid simply rides along. That's why the accuracy of aminoacyl tRNA synthetases, which load each tRNA with the right amino acid, matters so much.
links: tRNAs as adapters · Accuracy depends on tRNA synthetases

box: A cell runs short of free leucine, so many tRNAs whose anticodons read leucine codons stay uncharged.
claim: Ribosomes can skip the leucine codons and keep going in frame, making shorter proteins that lack leucine.
explanation: An uncharged tRNA has no amino acid to deliver. A ribosome that reaches a leucine codon waits, with that codon in its A site, until a charged tRNA arrives; it doesn't skip codons.
links: Charged vs uncharged tRNA · The A site

title: Which component is responsible?
prompt: Match each observation to the translation component that best explains it.

pairs.left: A mutant tyrosine tRNA inserts tyrosine at UAG stop codons, so some chains run on past them
A tRNA is loaded with the wrong amino acid but still pairs with the correct codon
An antibiotic binds rRNA in the large subunit and blocks peptide bond formation
In an extract missing one protein, finished chains stay attached to tRNAs at stop codons
A human mRNA without a 5' cap isn't translated in a human cell extract

explanation: Each component has one job: the anticodon decides which codon a tRNA reads (here, a mutant anticodon pairs with UAG); synthetases load the right amino acid; the rRNA peptidyl transferase center joins amino acids; release factors free the finished chain at a stop codon; eukaryotic initiation factors bring the small subunit to the 5' cap.
links: Components of translation

stem: The standard genetic code has 64 codons. How many of them are read by tRNAs carrying an amino acid?
explanation: Three codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop codons: no tRNA reads them, and a release factor binds instead. That leaves 61 codons for 20 amino acids, so most amino acids have several codons.
links: Stop codons · A redundant code

box: Suppose codons overlapped, so that bases 1-2-3, then 2-3-4, then 3-4-5 were each read as a codon.
claim: A single base change could then alter up to three neighbouring amino acids, whereas in the real code it alters at most one.
explanation: In an overlapping code each base belongs to three codons. Real codons are a nonoverlapping series of triplets, so each base sits in exactly one codon, and a base change can affect only that codon's amino acid.
links: Nonoverlapping triplets

stem: Which RNAs are made by transcription but never translated into protein?
options: mRNA and tRNA
mRNA only
tRNA and rRNA
rRNA and mRNA
tRNA only
explanation: Only mRNA carries a code that ribosomes translate. tRNA and rRNA are noncoding RNAs: they're transcribed from DNA (rRNA in the nucleolus) and work as RNA — tRNA as the adapter, rRNA as the ribosome's structural and catalytic core.
links: Central dogma · Noncoding RNAs · Ribosomes are RNA + protein

box: Translation is the last step in the flow of information from DNA to protein.
claim: Given a protein's amino acid sequence, you could work out the exact mRNA sequence that coded for it.
explanation: The code is redundant: most amino acids have two to six codons, so one protein sequence fits many possible mRNAs. Information can be read from codon to amino acid, but not reconstructed exactly the other way.
links: Redundancy of the code · Central dogma

box: A student is asked for the anticodon that pairs with the mRNA codon 5'-AUG-3'.
claim: Pairing base by base gives UAC, so written 5'→3' the anticodon is 5'-UAC-3'.
explanation: Pairing is antiparallel: the codon's first (5') base pairs with the anticodon's last (3') base. The anticodon is 3'-UAC-5', which written 5'→3' is 5'-CAU-3'.
links: Codon–anticodon pairing is antiparallel

title: Where can a ribosome start?
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Each coding bar is read from its AUG to the stop codon that follows.

(나) The inner AUG of mRNA 1 lies in the same reading frame as its first AUG.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: mRNA 2 can yield three separate polypeptides, because a ribosome can begin at each AGGAGGU sequence.
statements.explanation: Each coding region has its own Shine-Dalgarno sequence (AGGAGGU) upstream of its AUG, so one bacterial mRNA can code for several polypeptides.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: On mRNA 1, translation starts at the first AUG after the cap, and the inner AUG is read as methionine within the same polypeptide.
statements.explanation: The initiation complex assembles at the 5' cap and scans to the first AUG; a later AUG in the same frame simply codes for Met inside the chain.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: mRNA 1 comes from a bacterium, since it ends in a tail of A's.
statements.explanation: A 5' cap and a poly(A) tail are eukaryotic processing marks (Module 4). Bacterial mRNAs have no cap; mRNA 2's Shine-Dalgarno sequences mark it as bacterial.

links: Cap and scanning vs Shine-Dalgarno · Polycistronic mRNA

box: A researcher deletes only the first AGGAGGU sequence of mRNA 2 in the diagram.
claim: The first polypeptide stops being made, while the second and third are still translated.
explanation: In bacteria, each coding region's own Shine-Dalgarno sequence recruits a ribosome, which starts at the next AUG. Removing the first one blocks only the first region; the other two keep their binding sites.
links: Shine-Dalgarno sequence · Polycistronic mRNA

box: mRNA 1 in the diagram is added to a bacterial extract containing bacterial ribosomes and translation factors, but no eukaryotic initiation factors.
claim: The bacterial ribosomes can bind the cap and start translating at mRNA 1's first AUG.
explanation: Bacterial ribosomes find start sites by pairing with Shine-Dalgarno sequences, not caps, and mRNA 1 has none. That's why genes moved into bacteria are given a bacterial ribosome-binding sequence upstream of the AUG.
links: Shine-Dalgarno vs cap-dependent initiation

stem: Put these events of eukaryotic translation in order: (1) the large subunit joins; (2) the small subunit, initiation factors and Met-tRNA bind at the 5' cap; (3) the complex scans to the first AUG; (4) the first peptide bond forms.
explanation: The small subunit with Met-tRNA and initiation factors loads at the cap and scans; only when it reaches AUG does the large subunit join (and the factors leave). Peptide bonds form in the large subunit, so the first one comes last.
links: Eukaryotic initiation · Stages of translation

box: In the diagram, Met–Ala is attached to the tRNA in the P site, and a charged tRNA now enters the A site.
claim: When the next peptide bond forms, the new amino acid is added onto the chain, which stays attached to the P-site tRNA.
explanation: The reverse: the whole chain is transferred from the P-site tRNA onto the amino acid carried by the A-site tRNA. The chain (now Met–Ala–Trp) hangs from the A-site tRNA until the ribosome shifts one codon and moves that tRNA into the P site.
links: Elongation: transfer to the A-site tRNA · Translocation

stem: In the diagram, a tRNA enters the A site, a peptide bond forms, and the ribosome then shifts one codon. Which codons now sit in the E, P and A sites?
options: E: AUG, P: GCU, A: UGG
E: GCU, P: UGG, A: AAA
E: UGG, P: AAA, A: UAG
E: ACC, P: AUG, A: GCU
E: GCU, P: UGG, A: UAG
explanation: Translocation moves the ribosome one codon toward the 3' end: the tRNA on UGG (now holding the chain) moves to P, the empty tRNA on GCU moves to E, and the next codon, AAA, enters the A site.
links: Translocation by one codon · Ribosomes move 5'→3'

title: Endgame for this mRNA
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The ribosome continues along the mRNA until it reaches UAG.

(나) No tRNA has an anticodon that pairs with UAG.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: When UAG reaches the A site, a release factor protein binds there instead of a tRNA.
statements.explanation: Stop codons are recognized by a protein release factor, not by a tRNA.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: The chain is freed by breaking the peptide bond between its last two amino acids.
statements.explanation: Release breaks the bond between the finished chain and the tRNA holding it. All peptide bonds stay intact, and the last amino acid's carboxyl group becomes the C-terminus.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The ribosome will translate GCA, the codon after UAG, as alanine before it lets go.
statements.explanation: Translation ends at the stop codon; codons beyond it, such as GCA, aren't read.

links: Termination: release factor · Stop codons · C-terminus

box: Translation initiation differs between bacteria and eukaryotes.
claim: Elongation and termination differ just as much, since bacterial ribosomes lack A, P and E sites.
explanation: The differences are in initiation (cap and scanning vs Shine-Dalgarno sequences). Both kinds of ribosome have A, P and E sites, and elongation and termination work the same way.
links: Elongation and termination are shared

box: Electron micrographs often show several ribosomes spaced along one mRNA at the same time.
claim: Each ribosome makes only part of the polypeptide, and the pieces are joined together afterward.
explanation: Each ribosome starts at the start codon and runs to the stop codon, making its own complete chain. Several ribosomes on one mRNA simply make several copies at once.
links: Many ribosomes per mRNA · Ribosomes read 5'→3'

box: A mutation creates an extra AUG in the 5' untranslated region of a human mRNA, between the cap and the normal start codon, in a different reading frame.
claim: Scanning ribosomes can start at this new AUG instead, making a short, wrong polypeptide and less of the normal protein.
explanation: Eukaryotic ribosomes start at the first AUG they reach while scanning from the cap. An upstream AUG in another frame diverts them into the wrong reading frame — a known cause of some inherited diseases.
links: Scanning from the cap · Reading frame

box: A drug blocks only one step of translation: the large ribosomal subunit joining the small subunit at the start codon.
claim: Ribosomes already partway along an mRNA when the drug is added will finish their proteins, but no new proteins will be started.
explanation: Joining of the large subunit is part of initiation. Ribosomes already in elongation don't need that step again, so they run on to the stop codon; new rounds of initiation are blocked.
links: Three stages of translation

stem: A mutation changes codon 40 of a gene's 300 codons (counting AUG as codon 1) into UAG. What does the cell make from this mRNA?
options: A full-length chain lacking only its 40th amino acid
A 40-amino-acid chain ending in a special stop amino acid
No chain at all, since translation can't begin
A 39-amino-acid chain, freed when a release factor binds UAG
A full-length chain, since a tRNA reads UAG as an amino acid
explanation: Codons 1–39 are translated normally. UAG in the A site is recognized by a release factor (no tRNA reads it), so a shortened 39-amino-acid chain is released — usually nonfunctional.
links: Stop codons · Termination by release factor

title: Where does it happen?
prompt: Match each event to where it happens.

pairs.left: A charged tRNA first pairs with its codon
The tRNA holding the growing chain waits for the next amino acid
An uncharged tRNA leaves the ribosome
A eukaryotic ribosome first assembles on an mRNA
A bacterial ribosome first binds an mRNA

explanation: A = aminoacyl-tRNA entry, P = peptidyl-tRNA, E = exit. Eukaryotic initiation begins at the 5' cap and scans to AUG; bacterial ribosomes bind Shine-Dalgarno sequences (AGGAGGU) just upstream of each AUG.
links: A, P and E sites · Initiation in eukaryotes vs bacteria

title: Four snapshots at the ER
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Panels 1–4 follow one ribosome making one protein.

(나) In panel 1, the SRP is bound to the signal sequence as it emerges from the ribosome.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Translation pauses while the SRP is bound and resumes once the ribosome is handed to the channel.
statements.explanation: The SRP halts translation until the ribosome docks at the ER; when the SRP lets go, synthesis resumes and the chain is threaded through the channel.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Because the protein in panel 4 is in the ER lumen, it can only ever stay inside the ER.
statements.explanation: From the lumen, a protein may stay in the ER, travel in vesicles to another organelle's lumen (such as the Golgi or a lysosome), or be secreted (Module 3).

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The signal sequence lies at the protein's amino end, since it is the first part of the chain to emerge from the ribosome.
statements.explanation: Chains are made N-terminus first, so an amino-terminal signal is the first segment out — early enough to be caught before the protein is finished.

links: SRP targeting · Fates of rough-ER proteins (Module 3)

stem: In a mutant cell the SRP receptor is missing, but the SRP and the signal sequence are normal. What happens to a protein destined for secretion?
options: SRP still binds and pauses synthesis, but the ribosome can't dock at the ER
The SRP can't bind the signal sequence, so translation never pauses
The protein enters the ER normally, since the channel alone recognizes the signal
The protein enters the ER, but its signal sequence is never removed
The protein is redirected to the mitochondria by its signal sequence
explanation: The SRP recognizes the signal and halts translation, but docking requires the SRP receptor on the ER membrane. Without it, the ribosome is never handed to the channel, so the protein doesn't enter the ER or follow the secretory route.
links: SRP and SRP receptor · Translation starts in the cytosol

box: A secretory protein's gene is altered so that its ER signal sequence is deleted; nothing else changes.
claim: The protein will be made on free ribosomes and stay in the cytosol, since the SRP has nothing to recognize.
explanation: Translation always begins in the cytosol. Without a signal, the SRP never binds and the ribosome never goes to the ER; a protein with no signal remains in the cytosol.
links: No signal → cytosol · SRP needs the signal sequence

box: Panel 4 of the diagram shows the signal sequence as a separate fragment near the channel.
claim: So the mature protein in the lumen has lost amino acids from its carboxyl (C-terminal) end.
explanation: The signal sequence is the first part of the chain made, so it sits at the amino (N-terminal) end; cutting it off removes amino acids from the N-terminus. The mature protein is shorter than the chain the ribosome made.
links: Signal sequence at the N-terminus · Cleavage in the ER

title: Which end faces out?
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) The protein's orientation in the ER membrane is set while it is being made.

(나) It reaches the plasma membrane in vesicles that bud from one membrane and fuse with the next.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: The signal-anchor segment stays in the membrane because its side chains are mostly charged and cling to the phosphate heads.
statements.explanation: A segment spanning the membrane sits among the lipid tails, so its side chains are mostly nonpolar — the feature that marks integral membrane proteins (Module 3).

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Vesicle traffic turns the protein over, so the COO- end ends up outside the cell.
statements.explanation: Vesicles keep a protein's orientation: the COO- end, in the cytosol at the ER, stays in the cytosol at the plasma membrane.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: In the right panel, the NH3+ end lies in the extracellular fluid.
statements.explanation: Budding and fusion never flip a membrane: the side facing the ER lumen stays inside the vesicles and faces outside the cell after fusion (Module 3). So the N-terminus, in the lumen, ends up outside.

links: Signal-anchor sequence · The lumen side becomes the outside (Module 3)

box: Many plasma-membrane receptors carry sugar chains, which are attached in the lumen of the ER and Golgi.
claim: On the protein in the diagram, sugar chains attached in the ER lumen would end up on the NH3+ end's side of the membrane, outside the cell.
explanation: Sugars are added to the part of the protein facing the lumen — the NH3+ end's side. Through vesicle traffic that side becomes the outside face of the plasma membrane, which is why glycoprotein sugars face outward.
links: Membrane protein orientation · Glycoproteins face outward (Module 3)

title: Address labels
prompt: Match each protein to the sorting signal it needs.

pairs.left: A glycolysis enzyme that works in the cytosol
A citric acid cycle enzyme in the mitochondrial matrix
pairs.right: An amino-terminal signal for organelle import (made on free ribosomes)

pairs.left: A DNA polymerase that copies chromosomes
Albumin, a blood protein secreted by liver cells
pairs.right: An SRP-recognized ER signal, with no signal-anchor sequence

pairs.left: A receptor that spans the plasma membrane
pairs.right: An ER signal plus a signal-anchor sequence that keeps it in the membrane

explanation: Where a protein works decides its label: none for the cytosol; an amino-terminal signal for mitochondria or chloroplasts; an internal signal for the nucleus; an SRP-recognized amino-terminal signal for the ER and secretory route; and, for a protein that stays in a membrane, a signal-anchor sequence as well.
links: Signal sequences and destinations

stem: Stomach cells secrete pepsin as an inactive precursor, pepsinogen, which becomes active only after part of its chain is cut off in the acidic stomach. Which level of gene-expression control does this illustrate?
options: DNA accessibility
Transcription factors
RNA processing
Translation initiation at the cap
Post-translational modification
explanation: The protein is already made; activating it by cutting the chain is a post-translational modification. Making it inactive protects the cells that produce it from digesting their own proteins.
links: Post-translational modification · Real-world: digestive enzymes

box: A liver cell and a neuron from the same person carry the same genes but make very different sets of proteins.
claim: This is possible because the two cell types can read their genes with different genetic codes.
explanation: Both use the same standard code. They differ in which genes are expressed and how much, controlled at several levels: DNA accessibility, transcription factors, RNA processing and post-translational modification.
links: Levels of gene regulation · One genetic code

title: One gene, two cell types
stem: Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) In muscle cells, the gene for enzyme Z is wrapped tightly with histones and is never transcribed.

(나) In liver cells, the gene is transcribed and enzyme Z is made in an inactive form, switched on by phosphorylation when blood sugar drops.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: In muscle, expression of Z is blocked at the level of DNA accessibility.
statements.explanation: Tightly packed DNA can't be reached by the transcription machinery, so the gene stays silent.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: In liver, phosphorylation switches Z on without changing its amino acid sequence.
statements.explanation: Adding a phosphate group is a post-translational modification: the sequence stays the same, but the shape and activity change.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Muscle and liver cells can carry identical copies of the gene yet differ in whether they make active enzyme Z.
statements.explanation: All body cells carry the same genes; regulation decides which are expressed, and when.

links: Levels of gene regulation · Post-translational modification

box: In a human cell, an mRNA for a cytosolic protein is transcribed, processed, exported and translated.
claim: Ribosomes translate it inside the nucleus, so the protein is finished before the mRNA passes through a nuclear pore.
explanation: Transcription and processing (cap, tail, splicing) happen in the nucleus; the mature mRNA leaves through nuclear pores, and translation happens on ribosomes in the cytosol.
links: Overview of eukaryotic gene expression · Nuclear pores (Module 3)

title: Who goes where?
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Cyanobacteria use light energy to build sugars from CO2.

(나) Sulfur-oxidizing bacteria get energy by oxidizing hydrogen sulfide (H2S) and build sugars from CO2.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Both are phototrophs, since both make sugar from CO2.
statements.explanation: Making sugar from CO2 makes them both autotrophs. 'Phototroph' describes the energy source, and only the cyanobacteria use light.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Cyanobacteria belong in cell A and sulfur-oxidizing bacteria in cell B.
statements.explanation: Both take their carbon from CO2 (top row); cyanobacteria get energy from light (A), sulfur bacteria from a chemical compound (B).

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: A human belongs in cell C, since humans get their carbon from organic molecules.
statements.explanation: Humans do get carbon from organic molecules, but their energy comes from chemical compounds in food, not light — cell D.

links: Phototroph vs chemotroph · Autotroph vs heterotroph

box: Heliobacteria use light to make ATP but cannot fix CO2; they absorb organic molecules such as pyruvate as their carbon source.
claim: Heliobacteria belong in cell C of the diagram.
explanation: Energy from light puts them in the left column; carbon from organic molecules puts them in the bottom row: cell C, the photoheterotrophs.
links: Photoheterotrophs

stem: Using the diagram, a deep-sea vent bacterium builds all its organic molecules from CO2 and gets its energy by oxidizing hydrogen gas (H2). A fungus rotting a log gets both its energy and its carbon from the wood. Which cells do they belong in?
options: The bacterium in A; the fungus in D
The bacterium in B; the fungus in C
The bacterium in B; the fungus in D
Both in D, since neither uses light
The bacterium in D; the fungus in B
explanation: The vent bacterium: chemical energy + carbon from CO2 → B (a chemoautotroph, like the notes' hydrogen bacteria). The fungus: chemical energy + organic carbon → D (a chemoheterotroph); fungi are heterotrophs (Module 1).
links: Chemoautotrophs vs chemoheterotrophs · Fungi are heterotrophs (Module 1)

title: Where is the energy?
prompt: Match each example to the form of energy it best shows.

pairs.left: Water held behind a dam
The bonds of a glucose molecule
A sperm cell's beating flagellum
pairs.right: Kinetic energy: movement of a whole structure

pairs.left: Heat given off by a working muscle
pairs.right: Kinetic energy: random motion of molecules

pairs.left: A high concentration of Na+ outside a cell
pairs.right: Potential energy stored in a gradient

explanation: Potential energy is stored — by position, in bonds, or in a concentration difference; kinetic energy is motion, whether of a whole flagellum or of molecules jiggling as heat. One form converts into another: the dam's water spins a turbine, and the Na+ gradient powers transport (Module 3).
links: Potential vs kinetic energy · Chemical energy · Gradients (Module 3)

box: The notes link bond strength to potential energy: strong bonds hold less potential energy and weak bonds hold more.
claim: So a reaction that replaces weaker bonds with stronger ones ends with products of lower potential energy, releasing energy.
explanation: Stronger bonds store less potential energy. If the products are held by stronger bonds than the reactants, the difference is released — the hallmark of an exergonic reaction.
links: Bond strength and potential energy · Exergonic reactions

stem: Using the diagram, a mutation inactivates enzyme e2. Which molecule builds up first, and what can happen to it?
options: C builds up, since it can no longer be converted into D
A builds up, since B can no longer be made from it
D builds up, since nothing downstream uses it
B builds up, and more of it may flow to E and F
Nothing builds up, since each enzyme works independently
explanation: In a pathway, each product is the next step's reactant. With e2 gone, B can't become C, so B accumulates (and C and D run low); e4 can still use B, so the excess may flow toward E and F. Inherited diseases such as PKU work this way: a missing enzyme makes its substrate pile up and be diverted into side products.
links: Metabolic pathways · Real-world: inherited enzyme defects

box: The human brain is about 2% of body mass but uses about 20% of the body's energy at rest. Its neurons don't crawl, contract or divide.
claim: Since its neurons don't move, little of that energy can be going into cellular work; most must be lost directly as heat.
explanation: Cellular work isn't only movement: it includes pumping ions across membranes, making molecules such as proteins, and moving vesicles. Neurons spend much of their ATP on Na+/K+ pumps that restore the ion gradients they use to signal (Module 3).
links: Kinds of cellular work · ATP-driven pumps (Module 3) · Real-world: the brain's energy use

title: Build it up, break it down
stem: Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) After a meal, liver cells link glucose molecules into glycogen.

(나) During a fast, the same cells break glycogen back down into glucose.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Since (가) and (나) are reverse processes, running them back to back (glycogen → glucose → glycogen) costs the cell no usable energy.
statements.explanation: Every conversion loses some usable energy as heat (second law), so cycling between them always costs energy.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: (가) is anabolic and (나) is catabolic.
statements.explanation: Building a polymer from smaller units is anabolism; breaking it into smaller units is catabolism.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: (가) needs an input of energy, which cells supply by coupling it to ATP or a similar molecule.
statements.explanation: Anabolic reactions are endergonic. Linking sugars by condensation (Module 2) is driven by coupling it to the hydrolysis of phosphate bonds.

links: Anabolism vs catabolism · Condensation and hydrolysis (Module 2) · Second law

title: Reading the ATP diagram
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Each numbered bracket encloses one named molecule.

(나) x, y and z mark three bonds.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Bracket 3 encloses ADP, and bracket 2 encloses AMP.
statements.explanation: Adenine + ribose is adenosine (1); adding one phosphate gives AMP (2), two gives ADP (3), and three gives ATP (4).

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Hydrolyzing ATP to ADP + Pi breaks bond z.
statements.explanation: Removing the outermost phosphate breaks the bond between the second and third phosphates: z.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: At physiological pH each phosphate group is negatively charged, so the three phosphates repel one another.
statements.explanation: That crowding of negative charges is one reason ATP holds so much potential energy and its hydrolysis is exergonic.

links: ATP, ADP and AMP · ATP hydrolysis · Charge repulsion

box: Some reactions split ATP into AMP and pyrophosphate (two phosphates still joined together) instead of ADP + Pi.
claim: These reactions break bond y in the diagram rather than bond z.
explanation: AMP keeps only the phosphate nearest the ribose, so the break must come between the first and second phosphates — bond y — releasing the outer two phosphates together as pyrophosphate. RNA polymerase splits each incoming nucleotide the same way (Module 4).
links: ADP vs AMP · Pyrophosphate release (Module 4)

stem: According to the notes, which feature of ATP best explains why ATP + H2O → ADP + Pi releases energy at physiological pH?
options: Water is a high-energy molecule that passes its energy on to ATP
The bond between adenine and ribose holds most of ATP's energy
Its negative phosphates repel, so ADP + Pi has less potential energy
Its phosphates are uncharged and pack tightly, storing energy
The reaction is endergonic, so it takes in energy that the cell can then use
explanation: At physiological pH the phosphates are negatively charged and resist one another; splitting one off relieves that strain, so the products (ADP + Pi) have lower potential energy and the reaction is exergonic (−7.3 kcal/mol).
links: ATP hydrolysis is exergonic · Ionized phosphates (Module 2)

box: A sprinter's leg muscles hold only enough ATP for a few seconds of contraction, yet they can keep working far longer.
claim: This works because muscle cells store most of their energy as a large reserve of ATP.
explanation: Cells keep only a small amount of ATP and recycle it constantly: catabolism (breaking down sugars and fats) uses the energy it releases to rebuild ATP from ADP + Pi as fast as it's spent.
links: ATP is a currency, not long-term storage · Catabolism regenerates ATP

title: Pushing glucose uphill
stem: Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Glucose + Pi → glucose-6-phosphate + H2O, ΔG = +3.3 kcal/mol

(나) ATP + H2O → ADP + Pi, ΔG = −7.3 kcal/mol

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: On its own, (가) is endergonic and does not proceed spontaneously.
statements.explanation: A positive ΔG means the products have more free energy than the reactants.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: If the phosphate passes directly from ATP to glucose, the overall reaction glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP has ΔG = −4.0 kcal/mol.
statements.explanation: ΔG values of coupled reactions add: +3.3 + (−7.3) = −4.0 kcal/mol. The shared phosphate links the two reactions.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Coupling works because the enzyme lowers (가)'s ΔG from +3.3 to below zero.
statements.explanation: Enzymes never change ΔG. Coupling works by adding (가) to the more exergonic (나), so the combined ΔG is negative.

links: Energetic coupling · Enzymes don't change ΔG

stem: A biosynthetic step has ΔG = +10.0 kcal/mol. It can be coupled to the hydrolysis of ATP (−7.3 kcal/mol each). What is the smallest number of ATP that must be hydrolyzed to make the overall process spontaneous?
options: 1 ATP, giving a net ΔG of −2.7 kcal/mol
2 ATP, giving a net ΔG of −4.6 kcal/mol
1 ATP, since +2.7 kcal/mol is close enough
3 ATP, giving a net ΔG of −11.9 kcal/mol
None; an enzyme can lower the ΔG instead
explanation: One ATP gives +10.0 − 7.3 = +2.7 kcal/mol, still positive. Two give +10.0 − 14.6 = −4.6 kcal/mol, which is negative, so the coupled process can proceed. Enzymes don't change ΔG.
links: Energetic coupling arithmetic

box: A reaction has ΔG = +5.0 kcal/mol. A cell couples it to the hydrolysis of one ATP (ΔG = −7.3 kcal/mol), the two reactions sharing a phosphate intermediate.
claim: The coupled reaction has ΔG = −2.3 kcal/mol, so it proceeds spontaneously.
explanation: ΔG values of coupled reactions add: +5.0 + (−7.3) = −2.3 kcal/mol. A negative net ΔG makes the combined process exergonic.
links: Energetic coupling

stem: Which process does NOT require ATP (or another nucleoside triphosphate) as its energy source?
options: The Na+/K+ pump moving ions against their gradients
Linking amino acids into a growing polypeptide chain on a ribosome
Moving vesicles along cytoskeleton tracks
Adding nucleotides to a growing RNA strand
Glucose diffusing through a carrier, down its gradient
explanation: Facilitated diffusion is passive: glucose moves down its gradient, so no ATP is needed (Module 3). Pumping against a gradient, building proteins and RNA, and moving vesicles are all cellular work powered by ATP or other nucleoside triphosphates.
links: Cellular work · Passive vs active transport (Module 3)

box: Cells regenerate ATP by the reaction ADP + Pi → ATP + H2O.
claim: This reaction has ΔG = −7.3 kcal/mol, the same as ATP hydrolysis, so it runs on its own.
explanation: Reversing a reaction reverses the sign of ΔG: making ATP is +7.3 kcal/mol, endergonic. It happens only when coupled to energy released by catabolism, such as the breakdown of glucose.
links: Reverse reactions flip the sign of ΔG · Catabolism regenerates ATP

title: Reading two energy profiles
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Read all values from the free-energy axes.

(나) Both reactions run at the same temperature, with no enzyme.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Reaction I has ΔG = −40 kJ/mol, so it is spontaneous.
statements.explanation: ΔG = G(products) − G(reactants) = 20 − 60 = −40 kJ/mol: exergonic and thermodynamically favourable.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Reaction II has the lower activation barrier, so it is the spontaneous one.
statements.explanation: A low barrier makes a reaction fast, not favourable. Reaction II's products sit above its reactants (ΔG = 50 − 30 = +20 kJ/mol), so it is endergonic.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: The reverse of reaction II would have ΔG = −20 kJ/mol and an activation barrier of only 5 kJ/mol.
statements.explanation: Run backward, II starts at 50 and ends at 30 (−20 kJ/mol), and the climb from 50 to the peak at 55 is just 5 kJ/mol.

links: ΔG from free-energy profiles · Spontaneous ≠ fast · Activation energy

box: Reaction I in the diagram has a large, negative ΔG.
claim: So reaction I will proceed rapidly on its own as soon as the reactants are mixed.
explanation: ΔG tells whether a reaction can run on its own, not how fast. Reaction I must first climb a 50 kJ/mol activation barrier (60 → 110), which can make it very slow without a catalyst.
links: Spontaneous ≠ fast · Activation energy

stem: Using the diagram, what is reaction I's activation energy in the forward direction, and what would it be for the reverse reaction?
options: 50 kJ/mol forward; 90 kJ/mol reverse
110 kJ/mol forward; 90 kJ/mol reverse
50 kJ/mol in both directions
40 kJ/mol forward; 50 kJ/mol reverse
90 kJ/mol forward; 50 kJ/mol reverse
explanation: Activation energy is the climb from the starting level to the peak: forward 110 − 60 = 50 kJ/mol; in reverse, starting from the products, 110 − 20 = 90 kJ/mol. The reverse barrier is larger by exactly the size of ΔG (40 kJ/mol).
links: Activation energy · Transition state

box: A growing cell builds highly ordered proteins and membranes from simpler, more disordered molecules.
claim: This doesn't violate the second law, because the cell releases heat and simple waste molecules that increase the entropy of its surroundings by more.
explanation: The second law applies to the cell plus its surroundings. Order inside is paid for with energy from food or light, much of it released as heat and as CO2 and water, so total entropy still rises.
links: The second law and living systems · Entropy

stem: Muscle converts the chemical energy of glucose into movement with roughly 25% efficiency. What happens to the other 75%?
options: It's destroyed during the conversion, exactly as the second law states
It stays stored in the muscle as a reserve of extra ATP
It's converted back into glucose for later use
It leaves the muscle mostly in the form of light
It's released mostly as heat, raising entropy; none is destroyed
explanation: First law: energy is conserved, only converted. Second law: no conversion is 100% efficient, and the 'lost' energy is mostly heat that increases entropy — which is why exercise warms you and shivering keeps you warm.
links: First and second laws · Real-world: body heat

box: Dissolving the salt in an instant cold pack (ammonium nitrate) absorbs heat, with ΔH = +26 kJ/mol, but greatly increases disorder: TΔS = +33 kJ/mol at room temperature.
claim: ΔG for dissolving is −7 kJ/mol, so it happens spontaneously even though it absorbs heat.
explanation: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = +26 − 33 = −7 kJ/mol. A large enough increase in entropy can make a heat-absorbing process spontaneous.
links: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS · Real-world: cold packs

stem: A reaction has ΔH = −20 kJ/mol and makes things more ordered (ΔS < 0). Using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, what happens to its ΔG as temperature rises?
options: ΔG becomes more negative, since heat speeds up every reaction
ΔG doesn't change, since only ΔH determines ΔG
ΔG becomes less negative and eventually positive
ΔG becomes more negative, because T is measured in kelvin
The reaction becomes spontaneous only above some temperature
explanation: With ΔS negative, the −TΔS term is positive and grows with T, eating into the favourable ΔH, so the reaction is spontaneous only below some temperature. (Temperature also changes reaction speed, but that's about activation energy, not ΔG.)
links: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS · Temperature and entropy

box: In the blood, CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 (carbonic acid). During hard exercise, working muscles release more CO2 into the blood.
claim: The extra CO2 pushes this reaction back toward CO2 and water, raising the blood's pH.
explanation: Adding a reactant pushes a reversible reaction forward: more CO2 makes more H2CO3, which releases H+ (Module 2) and lowers the blood's pH slightly. The concentrations of reactants and products set the direction.
links: Concentrations set reaction direction · Acids and pH (Module 2)

box: The reaction A → B in a pathway has a positive ΔG when A and B are present at equal concentrations.
claim: A cell can still keep A → B running forward by keeping A plentiful and quickly using up B in the next step.
explanation: The notes give two ways cells run +ΔG reactions. One is to keep the reactant-to-product ratio above its equilibrium value — here by supplying A and draining B. The other is coupling to an exergonic reaction.
links: Running +ΔG reactions: concentrations · Metabolic pathways

box: A gazelle absorbs energy from the grass it eats. That energy ends up as movement, body heat, and chemical bonds in its tissues.
claim: Since much of it ends up as heat, the total energy in these forms is less than the energy absorbed; the rest was destroyed.
explanation: First law: energy is never destroyed. Movement + heat + stored chemical energy add up to everything absorbed. Heat is just the least useful form (second law), not missing energy.
links: First law: conservation of energy

box: Chlorophyll extracted from leaves glows red when lit in a test tube: its excited electrons drop back to lower energy levels with no chloroplast machinery to capture the energy.
claim: The red glow is the energy given off as the electrons fall back, which shows the energy is converted rather than destroyed.
explanation: When electrons move from higher to lower energy levels, the energy is released as heat or light — converted, not lost (first law). Inside a chloroplast, that same energy would be captured to make ATP and sugar instead.
links: Electrons dropping release energy · First law

stem: In CO2 + H2O → H2CO3, which description of the bonds is correct?
options: Every bond in both molecules breaks, and the atoms recombine at random
Water's bonds stay intact while the whole H2O molecule bonds to the carbon
Some of the carbon atoms are converted into oxygen atoms along the way
One C–O bond of CO2 and one O–H of water break; new C–O and O–H bonds form
No bonds break; the two molecules simply cling by hydrogen bonds
explanation: Atoms keep their identity; only bonds change. In the notes' example, one of the bonds between C and O in CO2 and one O–H bond in water break, and new bonds form between CO2's carbon and water's oxygen and between a CO2 oxygen and water's hydrogen.
links: Chemical reactions rearrange bonds, not atoms

box: In glycolysis, one step has a positive ΔG under standard conditions, yet it runs forward inside cells.
claim: This is possible because the enzyme for that step can make its ΔG negative.
explanation: Enzymes never change ΔG; they only lower the activation energy. The step runs forward because the next enzyme keeps using up its product, holding the product concentration low (other steps are pushed along by coupling to ATP).
links: Running +ΔG reactions · Enzymes don't change ΔG

stem: A firefly's light comes from a reaction that leaves a product molecule with an electron raised to a higher energy level. What actually produces the light?
options: New energy being created as the reaction's product bonds form
The excited electron falling back, releasing energy as light
Heat from the reaction making the insect's tissues glow
ATP being converted directly into light with no energy lost
Electrons being destroyed, releasing their energy as light
explanation: When an electron moves from a higher to a lower energy level, the difference is released as heat or light — here, mostly light. Chemical energy is converted into light energy, not created, and electrons aren't destroyed (first law); some energy is still lost as heat (second law).
links: Electrons dropping release energy · First law · Real-world: fireflies

title: Which way does the energy flow?
prompt: Match each process to the description of its energetics.

pairs.left: Building a protein from amino acids
pairs.right: Endergonic; joins monomers into a polymer (anabolic)

pairs.left: Oxidizing glucose to CO2 and water
pairs.right: Exergonic; catabolic, and its energy is used to remake ATP

pairs.left: ATP + H2O → ADP + Pi
ADP + Pi → ATP + H2O
Glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP
pairs.right: Coupled reaction with a negative net ΔG

explanation: Anabolic building needs energy (+ΔG); catabolic breakdown releases it (−ΔG), and cells capture some of it to remake ATP. ATP hydrolysis (−7.3 kcal/mol) is the exergonic half that cells couple to endergonic steps; running it in reverse flips the sign to +7.3; and adding the coupled ΔG values (+3.3 − 7.3) gives −4.0 kcal/mol.
links: Exergonic vs endergonic · Anabolism vs catabolism · Coupling

title: Two paths, one reaction
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Curves 1 and 2 show the same reaction, with and without an enzyme.

(나) a, b and c mark three energy differences.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Curve 2 is the enzyme-catalyzed path; adding the enzyme replaces barrier a with the smaller barrier b.
statements.explanation: Enzymes speed reactions by lowering the activation energy needed to reach the transition state.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: c is the same for both curves, so the enzyme doesn't change how much free energy the reaction releases.
statements.explanation: c is ΔG, set by the reactant and product levels; it is the same with and without an enzyme.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Because the enzyme is a folded protein, heating it until it unfolds would return the reaction to curve 1.
statements.explanation: The lower barrier depends on the active site, which exists only in the folded protein; a denatured enzyme no longer catalyzes (Module 5).

links: Enzymes lower activation energy · ΔG unchanged · Active site needs folding (Module 5)

box: In the diagram, c marks the free-energy difference between the reactants and the products.
claim: So this reaction is endergonic, and the enzyme supplies the energy it needs to proceed.
explanation: Products below reactants means a negative ΔG: the reaction is exergonic. Enzymes don't supply energy or change ΔG; they only lower the barrier (a → b).
links: Reading ΔG from a profile · What enzymes do

title: Three encounters at the enzyme
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) X resembles the substrate in shape.

(나) Y binds away from the active site and changes the enzyme's shape.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: Extra substrate would overcome Y's effect just as well, since Y also blocks the active site directly.
statements.explanation: Y is a noncompetitive inhibitor: it binds elsewhere and distorts the active site, so adding substrate can't push it out.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Adding a large excess of substrate could reduce X's effect, because substrate and X compete for the same site.
statements.explanation: X is a competitive inhibitor: the more substrate there is, the more often substrate rather than X wins the active site.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: If X binds only briefly and then falls off, its inhibition is reversible.
statements.explanation: Inhibitors that bind and come off again are reversible; those that bind permanently are irreversible.

links: Competitive vs noncompetitive inhibition · Reversible vs irreversible

box: Aspirin permanently attaches a small chemical group (an acetyl group) to an amino acid in the active site of the COX enzyme, which helps make inflammatory signals.
claim: Aspirin is therefore an irreversible inhibitor: the affected enzyme molecules stay inactive until the cell makes new ones.
explanation: A covalent change to the active site doesn't wear off, so the enzyme stays blocked; only newly made COX restores activity. Blood platelets have no nucleus and can't make new COX, which is why one aspirin's effect on them lasts for days.
links: Irreversible inhibition · Real-world: aspirin

stem: Methanol poisoning is treated with ethanol. Both are substrates of the same liver enzyme, which turns methanol into a toxic product. Which panel of the diagram best shows how ethanol helps?
options: Panel 2: ethanol competes with methanol for the active site
Panel 3: ethanol binds elsewhere on the enzyme and reshapes it
Panel 1: ethanol helps methanol fit into the active site
Panel 3: ethanol permanently destroys the enzyme
Panel 2: ethanol binds permanently, so no product forms
explanation: Ethanol and methanol fit the same active site, so plenty of ethanol keeps the enzyme busy (competitive inhibition) and slows toxic-product formation while the kidneys clear the methanol. Ethanol eventually leaves the site: the effect is reversible.
links: Competitive inhibition · Real-world: methanol poisoning

title: Brakes on a branched pathway
stem: Using the diagram, which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) D inhibits e2, the first enzyme on D's own branch.

(나) F inhibits e4, the first enzyme on F's own branch.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: When D is plentiful, B can still be used to make E and F instead of being spent on more D.
statements.explanation: Blocking e2 shuts only D's branch; B remains available to e4, so making F continues.

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: If D instead inhibited e1, a surplus of D would leave the making of F unaffected.
statements.explanation: e1 makes B, which both branches need. Inhibiting e1 would starve the F branch too — which is why feedback usually targets the first step after a branch.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: D must bind e2's active site in place of B, since feedback inhibition is a kind of competitive inhibition.
statements.explanation: End products usually look nothing like the first substrate; they typically bind a separate (allosteric) site and change the enzyme's shape, as isoleucine does to threonine dehydratase.

links: Feedback inhibition · Allosteric enzymes · Metabolic pathways

box: Isoleucine, the end product of a five-step pathway that starts from threonine, binds the pathway's first enzyme (threonine dehydratase) at a site separate from its active site.
claim: When isoleucine runs low, threonine dehydratase stays inhibited, because this kind of inhibition can't be reversed.
explanation: Allosteric feedback inhibition is reversible: as isoleucine is used up, it leaves the enzyme, the enzyme reactivates, and the pathway makes more. That's how the pathway matches supply to demand without wasting energy.
links: Feedback inhibition is reversible · Allosteric regulation

stem: In a single-chain enzyme, the three amino acids that form the active site are numbers 40, 95 and 210 in the sequence. How can residues so far apart work together?
options: Peptide bonds link them directly to one another
They lie next to each other in the primary structure
Folding brings them together in three-dimensional space
Each one comes from a different subunit
They pair with each other through hydrogen-bonded bases
explanation: The active site is formed by specific amino acids, often far apart in the sequence, that tertiary folding places side by side. Unfold the chain and the active site disappears.
links: Active site formed by folding · Tertiary structure (Module 5)

box: When glucose binds hexokinase, the enzyme's two lobes swing closed around it like a clamp.
claim: This fits the lock-and-key model better than induced fit, since the enzyme ends up perfectly shaped around glucose.
explanation: In the lock-and-key model the site already has the right shape. Hexokinase changes shape when glucose binds — the defining feature of induced fit.
links: Induced fit vs lock-and-key

stem: One molecule of an enzyme can convert thousands of substrate molecules per second. Which feature of the cycle E + S ⇌ ES ⇌ EP ⇌ E + P makes this possible?
options: The enzyme becomes part of each product molecule
The enzyme is released unchanged at the end of each cycle
Each cycle transfers energy from the enzyme to the substrate
The enzyme makes ΔG more negative, so products form instantly
The ES complex is permanent, so binding never has to repeat
explanation: After converting substrate to product in the active site, the enzyme lets the product go (EP → E + P) and is free to bind the next substrate. It is a catalyst: not consumed, not a source of energy, and no change to ΔG.
links: The enzyme–substrate cycle · Catalysts aren't consumed

box: Carbonic anhydrase speeds up CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 in body tissues and H2CO3 → CO2 + H2O in the lungs.
claim: One enzyme speeds both directions because it lowers the barrier for the forward and reverse reactions alike, while concentrations decide which way the reaction runs.
explanation: An enzyme lowers the transition-state peak, which both directions must cross. Where CO2 is high (tissues) the reaction runs forward; where CO2 is being breathed out (lungs) it runs backward.
links: Enzymes speed both directions · Concentrations set direction

title: What explains it?
prompt: Match each observation about an enzyme to the explanation that fits.

pairs.left: Boiling an enzyme destroys its activity for good
pairs.right: Heat unfolds the chain, destroying the active site

pairs.left: Mercury ions bond permanently to the enzyme's cysteines
A pathway's end product shuts down its first enzyme
pairs.right: Feedback inhibition of an allosteric enzyme

pairs.left: A substrate look-alike slows the reaction, but extra substrate overcomes it
A molecule binding away from the active site makes the enzyme work faster

explanation: Activity depends on the folded active site, which heat destroys. Permanent bonding = irreversible inhibition; product-triggered shutdown = feedback inhibition at an allosteric site; look-alikes compete for the active site; activators increase activity.
links: Enzyme regulation · The active site needs folding

box: Some drugs are designed to resemble a reaction's transition state rather than its substrate.
claim: Such drugs bind an enzyme's active site even more tightly than the substrate does, since the active site is shaped to stabilize the transition state.
explanation: Enzymes lower activation energy by binding and stabilizing the transition state. A stable look-alike of that state fits the active site best of all and blocks it — the design idea behind several drugs.
links: The active site stabilizes the transition state

stem: Which observation supports the induced-fit model rather than the lock-and-key model?
options: The substrate already fits the active site exactly before it binds
The enzyme acts on only one particular substrate
The enzyme speeds the reaction without being used up
ΔG is the same with and without the enzyme
The enzyme's shape changes measurably when the substrate binds
explanation: Both models explain specificity and catalysis; what sets induced fit apart is that binding itself reshapes the enzyme around the substrate. A perfect pre-existing fit is the lock-and-key picture.
links: Induced fit vs lock-and-key

title: Is every catalyst a protein?
stem: Which statements in <보기> are correct?
box:
(가) Module 6: chemical reactions in cells are catalyzed by proteins called enzymes.

(나) Module 5: the peptidyl transferase center that forms each peptide bond is made of rRNA.

statements.label: ㄱ
statements.text: (나) shows that at least one biological catalyst is an RNA molecule rather than a protein.
statements.explanation: The catalytic heart of the ribosome is rRNA, so 'enzymes are proteins' has an important exception (catalytic RNAs are called ribozymes).

statements.label: ㄴ
statements.text: Like a protein enzyme, the rRNA catalyst speeds peptide bond formation by lowering its activation energy, without changing its ΔG.
statements.explanation: Every catalyst works by lowering the barrier to the transition state; none changes the free-energy difference between reactants and products.

statements.label: ㄷ
statements.text: Because ribosomes contain RNA, they are membrane-bound organelles of the endomembrane system (Module 1).
statements.explanation: Ribosomes are RNA–protein complexes with no membrane. They are non-EMS whether free in the cytosol or bound to the ER (Module 1).

links: Ribozymes · Catalysts lower activation energy · Ribosomes are non-EMS (Module 1)
